messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kofi

Kofi was sixty-eight when the chemical storage facility caught fire at the Coast Guard station where he had worked for thirty-two years. The alarm sounded at 2:47 in the afternoon on a Tuesday in March, and within minutes the wind shifted, carrying a plume of acrid vapour across the dock where he stood. He remembered the burning sensation in his throat, the way his eyes began to water uncontrollably, and then—most vividly—the absolute silence that fell over the station as everyone froze, unsure whether to run or shelter in place. That silence had felt like the moment before something catastrophic, a held breath before the world broke. The exposure lasted only fifteen minutes before evacuation, but the chemical had lodged itself not just in his lungs but in the architecture of how he understood safety.

For the first few weeks after the incident, Kofi told himself he was fine. The medical clearance came through, his oxygen levels normalized, and he returned to his desk work at the administrative office. But something had shifted in how he inhabited the world. Four years later, at seventy-two, he found himself living in a state of perpetual vigilance that had quietly narrowed his life into something unrecognizable. The silence that had terrified him that afternoon—any silence, really—now triggered a cascade of physical symptoms: his heart would race, his palms would sweat, and a sense of impending doom would settle over him like a fog he couldn't name. Sitting in his living room in the evening when his wife, Ama, was reading quietly, Kofi would feel his body tense. The absence of sound had become a harbinger of danger, and he had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that threats lurked in the ordinary moments when nothing seemed to be happening. This conviction had taken root quietly, almost without his noticing, until it became the lens through which he filtered every experience.

The memories themselves were relentless. They returned unbidden—not as abstract recollections but as vivid, photographic scenes that played across his mind like a film he could not stop. He could see the exact colour of the sky that afternoon, the way the vapour looked like smoke, the expression on his supervisor's face. When these memories surfaced, they came with such overwhelming emotional force that Kofi had learned to simply stop whatever he was doing. He would sit very still, breathing shallowly, waiting for the wave to pass. Over time, he began to avoid anything that might trigger these replays. He stopped listening to the news—any report of an industrial accident could send him spiralling. He avoided the docks entirely, even though his office was nowhere near them. More subtly, he began to avoid his own thoughts about the event, believing with a kind of desperate certainty that if he allowed himself to think about what happened, he would not be able to handle the emotional onslaught. This conviction—that he lacked the capacity to bear even the slightest disturbance—had become a governing principle. Any small frustration with Ama, any minor inconvenience, felt like it might unravel him entirely, and so he had withdrawn further, speaking less, moving through the house like a ghost.

The memories triggered something deeper still: they reinforced his sense that danger was always present, always waiting. Each time the film played in his mind, each time he felt that photographic clarity of the moment, it seemed to confirm his darkest fear—that the world was inherently dangerous and that he was powerless to protect himself. This conviction then fed back into his threat sensitivity. The silence at home, which had once been peaceful, now felt ominous. He was on guard even inside his own house, listening for the sounds that did not come, interpreting their absence as a warning. Ama had begun to ask him what was wrong, why he seemed so distant, but he could not explain it to her. He could barely explain it to himself. What he knew was that something fundamental had broken in him that afternoon, and despite the years that had passed, despite the medical assurance that he was physically unharmed, he remained trapped in a loop where the memory of the event kept him hypervigilant, his hypervigilance convinced him the world was dangerous, and that conviction made him unable to tolerate even ordinary distress. It was Ama who finally insisted he see someone, after she found him sitting in the dark one evening, unable to explain why he had turned off all the lights, unable to articulate that the silence had become unbearable.
